2s Union filed written statement on 01.11.2023. Fact of the case which unfolds from in the written 
statement is that Binod Kumar Singh was a permanent employee of Eastern Coalfields Limited (hereinafter referred to 
as ECL). He was posted as a Driver at Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery under Bahula Area of ECL and died in harness on 
18.10.2016 leaving behind Rajesh Kumar Singh as his dependent son and Binda Kora as his widow. Rajesh Kumar 
Singh informed the management about death of his father and prayed for his employment as per provisions of 
National Coal Wage Agreement (hereinafter referred to as NCWA). The management held medical examination of 
the dependent son at Central Hospital, Kalla on 03.05.2017 and report was submitted in Form ‘O’. The dependent 
submitted his Transfer Certificate issued by the School, Aadhaar Card, PAN Card, Voter ID Card, Ration Card where 
his date of birth was recorded as 04.05.1983. According to Service Record Excerpt of his father his age was ten years 
on 11.03.1991. The contention of the union is that Rajesh Kumar Singh was thirty-three years five months and 
fourteen days on the date of death of his father and being below thirty-five years of age on the date of death of his 
father he is entitled to employment under ECL as per provisions of Clause 9.3.4 of NCWA union prayed for directing 
the management to provide employment to the dependent son, being the only son of the deceased employee and his 
mother having expired earlier. 


3. Management contested the case by filing their written statement on 04.12.2023. According to the 
management Rajesh Kumar Singh submitted an application for employment under the provision of NCWA. Due to 
absence of authentic documents in support of his age Rajesh Kumar Singh was referred to the Medical Board for his 
medical examination at Central Hospital, Kalla. On 03.05.2017, after examination a report was submitted where the 
age of Rajesh Kumar Singh was assessed between 35 to 40 years. According to the management the mid-point of age 
is considered as age of the applicant on the date. Accordingly, the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh is calculated as thirty- 
seven years and six months on 03.05.2017 and he was found to be above the age of thirty-five years on the date of 
death of his father and therefore he is not eligible for employment as per provisions of 9.3.4 of NCWA. 


4. Union examined Rajesh Kumar Singh as Workman Witness No. 1. The witness field his affidavit-in-chief 
where he stated that his father died on 18.10.2016 while he was in the service of the company. As a dependent he 
filed an application for providing employment to him as per provisions of NCWA. After proper screening at the 
Colliery and Area Level he appeared for his Initial Medical Examination (hereinafter referred to as IME) before the 
IME Board at Central Hospital, Kalla. After medical examination the assessed age was not disclosed to him and the 
proposal for his employment was not processed on the ground that he was over-age. It is further stated that the 
management served a copy of letter addressed to the Personnel Manager (IC) where it was communicated to him that 
Rajesh Kumar Singh was over-age and he was not entitled to employment. The union stated that according to various 
documents his date of birth appeared as 04.05.1983. As per Service Records of his father management recorded the 
age of Rajesh Kumar Singh as ten years on 11.03.1991. Even his Birth Certificate disclosed that his date of birth is 
04.05.1983. According to the workman witness his age was 33 years 5 months and 14 days on the date of death of his 
father and being below 35 years, he stood eligible for employment. According to the witness IME Board deliberately 
decided his age above 35 years on the date of assessment without considering the Service Record and other 
documents. The witness asserted that his date of birth appearing in the Transfer Certificate issued by his School and 
Birth Certificate as well as the age recorded in the Service Record of his father should be accepted for providing 
employment to him. The workman witness produced the following documents in support of his case : 


(i) Copy of the Death Registration Certificate of Binod Kumar Singh is produced as Exhibit W-1. 


(ii) Copy of application of Rajesh Kumar Singh addressed to the Agent, Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery, 
informing his father’s death, as Exhibit W-2. 


(iii) Copy of the Service Book of Binod Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-3. 


(iv) Copy of the letter of Assistant Manager (Personnel), Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery addressed to the Chief 
Manager (Personnel), Bankola Area, for IME of Rajesh Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-4. 


(v) Copy of the No objection certificate in respect of Rajesh Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-5. 
(vi) Copy of the Birth Registration Certificate of Rajesh Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-6. 
(vii) Copy of the Aadhaar Card of Rajesh Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-7. 


(Vili) Copy of the letter of the Sr. Manager (Personnel) Empl/ED addressed to the Sr. Manager 
(Personnel)/IC, Bankola Area for re-assessment of age of Rajesh Kumar Singh, as Exhibit W-8. 


(ix) Copy of the Transfer Certificate of Rajesh Kumar Singh issued by Fuleshwari Devi Memorial High 
School, as Exhibit W-9. 


3: In cross-examination the witness admitted his signature on Exhibit M-1, a letter dated 05/11.08.2017 issued 
by the Sr. Manager (Personnel)/IC, Bankola Area addressed to the Agent, Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery wherein it was 
communicated that the Apex Medical Board assessed the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh on the date of death of Binod 
Kumar Singh as 36 years 11 months and 15 days, as such he is not eligible for employment as per NCWA. The age 
assessment report of Rajesh Kumar Singh has been marked as Exhibit M-2. It appears from the said document that his

age was assessed as 35 to 40 years as on 03.05.2017 by way of holding X-Ray of the Lateral Spinal Cord, Mandible, 
Laryngeal Cartilage and Skull. Witness denied the suggestion that his claim for employment is not maintainable. 


6. Management examined Mr. Anuj Lakra, Manager (Personnel), Nakrakonda — Kumardihi ‘B’ Collieries as 
Management Witness No. 1. The witness in his affidavit-in-chief has reiterated the case disclosed by the management 
in their written statement. According to the witness the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh on 03.05.2017 was assessed 
between 35 to 40 years and it was communicated to him that he was disqualified for his employment due to over-age. 
In his evidence-in-chief Management Witness No. | deposed that Rajesh Kumar Singh exceeded the age for 
employment and for such reason his prayer for employment was regretted. The witness further deposed that Rajesh 
Kumar Singh was 36 years 11 months and 15 days of age at the time of death of his father and was not eligible for 
employment. 


7. In cross-examination the witness deposed that the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh was assessed in proper 
manner. The witness denied that the documents produced by Rajesh Kumar Singh showed that his age was below 35 
years on the date of death of his father. 


8. The point of contention in this case is whether the management of Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery, Bahula Area, 
ECL is justified in not providing employment to Rajesh Kumar Singh on compassionate ground and what relief the 
dependent son of the deceased is entitled to. 


9. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative advancing his argument submitted that according to the provisions 
of Clause 9.3.2 of NCWA the dependent son of the deceased employee is entitled to compassionate appointment on 
the death of his father. Clause 9.3.4 prescribes that for grant of compassionate appointment the concerned dependent 
should be physically fit and suitable for employment with age not more than 35 years. It is submitted that the 
dependent son by his letter dated 21.10.2016 informed the Agent / Manager, Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery about the death 
of his father on 18.10.2016 and prayed for employment.A copy of letter is produced as Exhibit W-2. The dependent 
son was asked to appear before the screening committee of the management and thereafter his medical examination 
was held on 03.05.2017 where his age was assessed as 35 to 40 years. It is argued that as per Service Record the age 
of the dependent son was 33 years and 6 months on the date of death of his father. Mr. Rakesh Kumar heavily relied 
upon the Birth Certificate and School Leaving Certificate of Rajesh Kumar Singh which have been produced as 
Exhibit W-6 and W-9 respectively, where the date of birth is recorded as 04.05.1983. It is submitted that the deceased 
employee left behind Sarita Devi, a married daughter who had submitted her no objection in favour of his brother and 
the same is produced as Exhibit W-5. The union representative strenuously argued that when the School Leaving 
Certificate and Birth Registration Certificate were produced the management should have considered the same for 
determination of age and management should consider the guidelines laid down in Annexure-I of Implementation 
Instruction No. 76 of NCWA, relating to procedure for determination and verification of age. It is submitted that in 
case of non-matriculate but educated candidates where the candidate pursued studies in a recognized educational 
institution, the date of birth recorded in the School Leaving Certificate should be treated as correct date of birth and 
the same will not be altered under any circumstances. It is argued that in the instant case Rajesh Kumar Singh studied 
up to Class-IX at Fuleshwari Devi Memorial High School at Ukhra, Burdwan and is a literate person. Therefore, 
management should consider his date of birth as 04.05.1983 appearing in the Transfer Certificate / Schlool Leaving 
Certificate for the purpose of his employment. It is argued that the dependent son is entitled to employment. 


10. Mr. P. K. Goswami, learned advocate for the management of ECL argued that according to the Service Book 
of the deceased employee (Exhibit W-3), the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh was recorded as 10 years as on 11.03.1991. 
Therefore, his age may be computed as 35 years and 7 months on the date of death of his father on 18.10.2016. 
Learned advocate referred to the IME report (Exhibit M-2), where after holding X-ray examination of various parts of 
body the IME Board assessed the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh as 35 to 40 years on the date of examination 1.6., 
03.05.2017. It is argued that as per rules the mid-point of the assessed age is considered to be the age of the person on 
the date of examination and it is abundantly clear that the dependent son of the deceased employee is more than 35 
years of age on the date of death of his father and he was not eligible for employment as per Clause 9.3.4 of NCWA. 
Learned advocate argued that the Birth Certificate (Exhibit W-6) and Transfer Certificate (Exhibit W-9) are not 
reliable documents as the Birth Certificate was obtained in the year 2014 and it is not a cotemporaneous document. 
The union has not examined the Headmaster of the School to establish the date of birth appearing in the Transfer 
Certificate based upon the date appearing in the Admission Register. It is further argued that Annexure-I of the 
Implementation Instruction No. 76 of NCWA is applicable to the employees of the company for determining any 
dispute regarding their age and the same terms do not apply to the person claiming employment for the first time. 
Learned advocate submitted that the candidate claiming employment was informed by the management by letter dated 
05/11.08.2017 (Exhibit M-1) and 09.07.2018 (Exhibit W-8) that the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh was assessed by 
Central Hospital, Kalla and his proposal for employment is regretted for being over-age. It is argued that the 
dependent is not entitled for any employment. 


11. Perused the pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and rival arguments advanced on behalf of the union 
and management. The bone of contention is whether the dependent son had already attained the age of 35 years on the 
date of death of his father, on 18.10.2016 and he is entitled to compassionate appointment under Clause 9.3.4 of 


7830 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 10, 2026/PAUSHA 20, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


NCWA. It is a well settled law that NCWA is a settlement under Section 2(p) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and 
is binding upon the employer and employees under Section 18(3) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The binding effect 
of NCWA has been discussed and clearly spelt out by the Hon'ble High Court at Calcutta in the cases of Eastern 
Coalfields Limited Vs. Kumari Kiran Singh and Others [AIRONLINE 2018 CAL 1593] and Sukumoni 
Hembram alias Sukumoni Mejhan Vs. Union of India and Others [MAT 27 of 2024]. Since the terms and 
conditions for granting employment to the dependent has been specified in the provisions of NCWA, any deviating 
from such terms is permissible for the purpose of granting employment to a person claiming for employment as a 
dependent. In the instant case initiating the process for employment of Rajesh Kumar Singh, management held age 
assessment through the Medical Board on 03.05.2017. The concerned dependent did no raise any objection against 
holding of age assessment examination by the Medical Board of the employer company. It appears from Exhibit M-2 
that scientific investigation was carried out for the purpose of assessing the age according to medical jurisprudence 
and his age was assessed between 35 to 40 years. The accepted position is that the midpoint of the range of age is 
accepted to be the age of a person for all functional purpose. Accordingly, it transpires that Rajesh Kumar Singh was 
36 years and 11 months on the date of death. From the Service Book of the deceased employee (Exhibit W-3) it is 
gathered that the age of Rajesh Kumar Singh was recorded as 10 years as on 11.03.1991, therefore his age on the date 
of death of his father can be assessed as 35 years, 7 months and 7 days and he is therefore found over-age for his 
employment. The union has produced two other relevant documents in support of the age of the claimant. A Birth 
Registration Certificate issued by Munger District Gram Panchayet Office, Government of Bihar dated 11.08.2014 
where the registration appears to have been made on 09.08.2014. The date of birth recorded in the certificate as 
04.05.1983 cannot be considered as sacrosanct as the registration has been made after a lapse of thirty-one years and 
the contents of such certificate which is not contemporaneous is only based upon hearsay material. The Transfer 
Certificate which is heavily relied upon by the union has been admitted in the evidence as Exhibit W-9. The document 
reveals that at the time of leaving the school on 30.04.1997 he was studying in Class-VIII and was promoted to Class- 
IX. The Headmaster of the School was not summoned by the union for proving the contents of the Transfer 
Certificate. The Admission Register was not produced for verification of such certificate. Under such circumstances I 
am not inclined to place reliance upon the Transfer Certificate for the purpose of accepting 04.05.1983 as the date of 
birth of Rajesh Kumar Singh. 


12. The union representative argued that Clause A (ii) of Annexure-I of the Implementation Instruction No. 76 of 
NCWA has to be followed for determining the age of non-matriculate but literate candidate by accepting the date of 
birth of the candidate appearing in the School Leaving Certificate. On a careful consideration I find that 
Implementation Instruction No. 76 is a part of NCWA and provides procedure for resolving age dispute of the 
employees and it also deals with various situation where the appointee is a matriculate, non-matriculate but educated, 
ex-serviceman, or an illiterate person. In my considered view such provisions are not applicable to persons who claim 
compassionate appointment. A claimant in order to succeed must strictly prove that he has fulfilled all the required 
terms and conditions for compassionate employment. In the present case the union has failed to prove that the 
dependent son was below 35 years of age on the date of death of his father. Therefore, I hold that Rajesh Kumar 
Singh is not entitled to compassionate employment under Clause 9.3.4 of NCWA. The management’s case is fortified 
by the report of IME as well as Service Book which prove that the claimant was over-age on 18.10.2016. The 
decision of the management of Kumardihi ‘B’ Colliery, Bankola Area, ECL in not providing employment to Rajesh 
Kumar Singh on compassionate ground is consistent with the facts and circumstances of the case and the provisions 
of NCWA binding the parties. The dependent son is consequently not entitled to any relief in this case. The Industrial 
Dispute is liable to be dismissed on contest. 


Hence, 
ORDERED 


that the Industrial Dispute is dismissed on contest. Rajesh Kumar Singh, dependent son of the deceased 
employee, Binod Kumar Singh is not entitled to any relief and I find no illegality in the action of management of 
Eastern Coalfields Limited in not providing employment to the son. Let an award be drawn up in light of my above 
findings. Let copies of the Award in duplicate be sent to the Ministry of Labour, Government of India, New Delhi for 
information and Notification.

As per letter dated 10/01/2019 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
22012/166/2018 (IR(CM-II)) dt. 10/01/2019. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“WHETHER THE ACTION ON THE PART OF SUB AREA MANAGER SECL, RAJGAMAR 
COLLIERY IN NOT MAKING O.T PAYMENT ON THE BASIS OF O.T SLIP PEREORMED BY SHRI 
D.P. SARAF, EX- CHIEF STORE KEEPER AND JOINT SECRETARY OF RASTRIYA COLLIERY 
MAZDOOR CONGRESS AS PER THE ACTUAL ०.7 HOURS PERFORMED DURING THE PERIOD 
FROM 13-05-2013 TO 30-07-2017 IS APPROPRIATE AND JUSTIFIED? IF NOT, WHAT RELIEF 
SHRI D.P.SARAF, EX- CHIEF STORE KEEPER AND JOINT GENERAL SECRETARY OF RCMC IS 
ENTITLED TO?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, he has been appointed as Chief Storekeeper with the Management 
from 13.05.2013 to 30.06.2017 and has superannuated on 30.06.2017 after completing the age for superannuation. 
While in his posting he was instructed by Management to collect different articles from Regional Store Korba Area, 


7832 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 10, 2026/PAUSHA 20, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Central Warehouse Korba and Central Store which were about 17 to 18 kilometers from the place of his posting in 
Rajgamar. He was not provided any vehicle for this purpose. As per rules he is required to work only for six and half 
hours a day and is entitled to overtime for any hour in excess of this six and half hours period. He had to work for 
more than six and half hours prescribed for execution of the directions of Management to fetch the articles from these 
stores, and deposit them with Rajgamar store. He used to mention the time when he proceed to these stores and 
returned back to Rajgamar as well remained in the Rajgamar Office, which has been destroyed by Management. He 
had prepared worksheet mentioning the hours he worked, which was not counter signed by the Office of Management 
and when he claimed over time dues for the work he did in cases of his prescribed working hours, his this demand 
was also refused by the Management which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. Thus, he has claimed that Management be 
directed to pay him the amount calculated by him as overtime with interest and fine. 


Case of Management is that, the Management used to send the Workman from Rajgamar Colliery to 
different stores mentioned by him for collecting articles for which he produced his TA bills and his expenses were 
reimbursed on the basis of his TA bills. It is further the case of the Management that, when a person is sent to another 
place for official job, he is required to be paid his travelling expenses and DA for the job date. There is no provision 
of payment of overtime allowances in such cases. Management has thus prayed that reference be answered against the 
Workman. 


Both the sides have filed affidavits and documents, which are different orders of Management directing him 
to visit the stores and collect the articles, TA Bills of the Workman. 


I have heard the Workman in person and Learned Senior Counsel Mr. Anoop Nair for the Management 
assisted by Learned Counsel Mr. Neeraj Kewat. I have gone through the record as well. 


The main argument from the side of Management is that, there is no provision for payment of overtime to a 
workman who is sent to a place different than the place where he is posted. In such cases, as per Rules the Workman 
is reimbursed his travelling expenses and TA for the date subject to Rules. 


Coal India Travelling Allowances Rules, 2010 
Para 10.2.2 & 10.2.5 requires to be referred in this respect and is being reproduced as follows: 
10.2.2 When the distance between the two places is 32 kilometers or less :- 


The amount reimbursable shall be the actual fare, by stage carriage (e.g. a bus) for non- 
executive cadre employees drawing pay less than Rs. 23479.55/- per month and in cases of other non- 
executive & executive cadre employees including Management Trainees, the actual fare provided that the 
journey is performed by taxi, auto-rickshaws, deluxe buses, AC buses etc. 


Note: Non-executive cadre employees drawing pay Rs.22149.01/- per month and above will be 
entitled to travel by the upper class in a stage carriage where more than one class is provided. They will be 
entitled to travel by deluxe buses also. (Authority: No. CIL/C-SA(PC)/ TA-2010/164 Date: 03.10.2012) 

Perusal of these Rules, makes it clear that there is no provision of payment of overtime in such 
situation. 


10.2.5 Reimbursement of local traveling expenses (RLTE) to employees for attending duties on 
Sundays/Holidays or during odd hours on working days: 


Reimbursement at the rate specified in Rule 10.2.1/10.2.2 from residence to place of duty and 
back, will be allowed subject to following conditions: 


a) Nosuch reimbursement will be allowed if Over Time Allowance has been paid or compensatory leave 
is allowed for duties performed. 


b) Odd hours for this purpose will be reckoned from 8-00 p.m. to 8-00 a.m. 


c) Where the journey by train is involved, reimbursement of Taxi/Auto fare or stage carriage charges 
will be limited to connecting distances between place of duty/place of residence and Railway station 
besides the Railway fare as per entitled class. 


(d) No employees will be entitled for reimbursement of local travelling expenses (RLTE) for attending 
duties on Sundays, Holidays or during odd hours on working days from residence to office and back. 
However, Executives will be reimbursed RLTE if they are on official duty from office to any other 
place. 


Hence, in the light of above discussion, holding the action of Management in not granting the 
Workman overtime for the extra hours on work since he was paid travelling allowances when he was sent to 
some other places for collection of materials by Management is held just, legal and proper and the reference 
stands answered accordingly.

(JUDGMENT) 


(Passed on this 13 “day of November - 2025) 


As per letter dated 05/11/2012 of the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
22012/136/2012 (IR(CM-I)) dt. 05/11/2012. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of General Manager, Kusmunda Area of SECL, District Korba 
(CG) not given the notional seniority in EP Fitter cum Mechanic Grade-I, in Category-'B' to Shri S.R. 
Maneshwar of Kusmunda Area as per the Arbitration award with effect from 23.12.1988 at par as given to 
their after workmen in SECL Gevra Area was legal and justified? What relief the said workman is entitled 
to and from what date?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared 
and filed their respective statement of claim and defense. 


7834 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 10, 2026/PAUSHA 20, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


The undisputed facts are that, the Applicant Workman Shesh Ram Maneshwar was appointed in the Korba 
West Area of SECL as Mechanic (trainee) along with three other workers namely Dhani Ram Patle, L.P. Rahangdale 
and Lakhan Lal Jhothe vide appointment letter dated SECL/GM/KB(W)/PM/APPMNT/87/3977 dated 12.11.1987. 
Later on, the Korba West Area was split into three different areas viz; Gevra, Kusmunda and Korba. The three 
Workmen i.e. Dhani Ram Patle, L.P. Rahangdale and Lakhan Lal Jhothe were posted in Gevra Area whereas the 
Applicant Workman was posted in Kusmunda Area. Dhani Ram Patle claimed notional seniority before the 
Management and his case was sent for joint arbitration. Award dated 23.12.1992 was passed by the Arbitrators 
holding the Workman Dhani Ram Patle entitled to be regularized as Fitter cum Mechanic Grade-I in Group — B on 
completion of his successful one year training. The remaining two workers i.e. L.P. Rahangdale and Lakhan Lal 
Jhothe also claimed the same regularization on the basis of Arbitration Award and they were promoted notionally in 
seniority in Grade — I Group - B wee.f. 23.12.1988 vide Office order No. SECL/DGM/GBR/95/4021. The 
Management refused same benefit to the Applicant Workman on the ground that he was posted in Kusmunda Area of 
the Company and not in the Gevra Area where other workmen, who were benefited, were posted. The Management 
further took the ground that, the Award was with respect to Workman D.R. Patle only posted in Gevra Area and 
because it will disturb the settled seniority list in the Kusmunda where the applicant workman is posted. Another case 
of Management is that, the claim is barre,d by unexplained delay and latches. 


The Workman side has filed Office Order dated 10.11.1995/12.12.1995 regarding promotion of L.P. 
Rahangdale and Lakhan Lal Jhothe w.e.f. 23.12.1986 with D.R. Patle as per arbitration Award, Copy of petition 
before Labour Commissioner, reply of Management, Rejoinder of Union, Failure report which are Exhibit W-1 to W- 
6. Management has filed the memorandum of settlement with regard to promotion of L.P. Rahangdale and Lakhan Lal 
Jhothe in the light of Award with respect to D.R. Patle. An Office Order dated 10.11.1995/12.12.1995 which have 
been filed by the Workman Union also. 


Both the sides have filed affidavit with respect to their claims and defense. It also appears that, the 
Workman died during the pendency of the Case but since the case is espoused by the Union and Act specifically 
provides that no reference was abated on the basis of Claimant Workman. This reference will also not abate. 


None was present for Workman Union at the time of argument. I have heard argument of Learned Counsel 
Mr. Neeraj Kewat for the Management and I have gone through the record. 


From perusal of record, it establishes that four persons including the claimant workman were appointed on 
one day in Korba West Area and worked together in the same area, later on this Korba Area was divided into three 
areas. Three employees went to Gevra Area and the claimant Workman was absorbed in the Kusmunda Area. Three 
co-workers of the Claimant Workman with identical claims were granted their claims by the Management were else 
the claimant workman was refused the relief on the ground that he was in a different area. It is not disputed all these 
areas are controlled and managed as well governed by the one Company South Eastern Coal Field Limited which is 
itself a subsidiary of Coal India. In these circumstances, refusal of relief of promotion as claimed by the Claimant 
Workman in parity with other beneficiaries, who had identical claims, only on the ground that it will disturb the 
settled seniority list in the area is nothing but arbitrary and is in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. 


Hence, in the light of above discussion and findings the Claimant Workman Shesh Ram Maneshwar is 
also held entitled to be promoted from Fitter cum Mechanic Grade-I Category-C to Category-B after 
completion of his successful training of one year i.e. from 23.12.1988 in parity with the Workman Dhani Ram 
Patle, L.P. Rahangdale and Lakhan Lal Jhothe and is held entitled to get all benefits in this respect from 
Management accordingly treating him to be notionally promoted from 23.12.1988. However, the mandatory 
benefits could be given from 12.12.1995 i.e. the date of promotion of other co-workers mentioned above. 


The reference stands answered accordingly. 
AWARD 


Holding the action of the management of General Manager, Kusmunda Area of SECL, District Korba 
(CG) not given the notional seniority in EP Fitter cum Mechanic Grade-I, in Category-'B' to Shri S.R. Maneshwar 
of Kusmunda Area as per the Arbitration award with effect from 23.12.1988 at par as given to their after workmen 
in SECL Gevra Area illegal, arbitrary and unjustified, he is held entitled to get all benefits in this respect from 
Management accordingly treating him to be notionally promoted from 23.12.1988. However, the mandatory 
benefits could be given from 12.12.1995 i.e. the date of promotion of other co-workers mentioned above. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 25/07/2012 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-10 of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-22012/86/2012(IR(CM-IT)) dt. 25/07/2012. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“Whether the action of the General Manager, Central Workshop, Jayant Project of NCL, in imposing 
punishment of Suspension, Stoppage of increment & Penal rent, on an alleged misconduct of illegal 
occupying of the quarter by Shri J.P. Singh, Fitter (vacated during the course of enquiry proceedings), is 
legal and justified? To what relief the claimant is entitled for, and from which date?” 


7836 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 10, 2026/PAUSHA 20, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


The case of the workman is mainly that while he was working as Fitter with the management, he was 
issued a charge sheet alleging misconduct under clause 26.14 of certified standing orders on his part by way of 
illegally and unauthorizedly breaking open residential accommodation MQ-463 of management and occupying it 
illegally without any allotment in his favour. This charge sheet dated 11.09.2000 was replied by him but ignoring his 
reply, the management conducted an enquiry with respect to the allegations arbitrarily and without observing 
principles of natural justice. Charges were wrongly held proved and the punishment in form of stoppage of one 
increment with cumulative effect as well penal rent imposed on the workman is also excessive to the misconduct. 


The workman has prayed that holding this action of management against law and unjustified, the punishment 
be set aside. 


Case of the management is that the workman has been in habit of committing misconduct, he was issued a 
charge sheet on 12.07.1995 alleging misconduct as defined under clause 26.3, 26.5, 26.16 and 26.22 of certified 
standing orders, which were enquired into and after the charges were proved in enquiry he was punished. He did not 
improve himself and repeated the misconduct in the year 2000 by way of unauthorizedly and illegally breaking open 
the company’s accommodation No. 459-Q forcibly and taking illegal possession in the said residence which is 
misconduct under clause 26.14 of certified standing orders, after his reply was found in sufficient, an enquiry was 
conducted, as per rules the workman was found guilty of misconduct in the enquiry and he was punished, which is not 
excessive to the misconduct proved and keeping in view the fact that he is a habitual offender; management has 
requested that the reference be answered against the workman. 


Following Preliminary Issue was framed on the basis of pleadings:- 
Whether the departmental enquiry conducted is legal and proper? 


On the basis of evidence, this issue was answered vide order dated 23.02.2024, the departmental enquiry 
was held vitiated in law, management was granted opportunity to prove the charge before this Tribunal. This order is 
part of this judgment and award. 


The management filed affidavit of its witness Anand Murti, General Manager in support of charge as his 
Examination-in-chief. He was cross-examined by workman side, he has proved the documents which were proved 
during the hearing of preliminary issue. 


No evidence in rebuttal was filed by workman. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. Neeraj Kewat, Learned 
Counsel for the management. I have gone through the record as well. 


On perusal of record in light of rival arguments, following Issues came up for determination:- 


4) Whether the charges are proved from the evidence before this Tribunal? 
2) Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charges proved? 
Issue No.1, 


Charges have been elaborated earlier, the management witness has stated that the workman entered in 
quarter No. MQ-463 illegally after breaking lock, inspite of the fact that he was allotted quarter No. MQ-458 and 
occupied the said quarter No. MQ-463 illegally. He referred to document M-E/9 entry dated 16.03.1989 in this 
respect which is handing over or taking over register. This witness also states that later on the workman vacated the 
MQ-463 which he had illegally occupied after breaking open its lock. An enquiry was conducted in this respect and 
was punished with permanent stoppage of one increment and deduction of penal rent for illegally occupying for the 
period he had illegally occupied the accommodation. 


There is nothing in his cross-examination to discredit this witness. 


The case of the workman is that he was entitled to one accommodation from the company residence 
which was vacant, it has been the practice and it is usual for the employees who break open the vacant residence and 
enter. Thereafter, the company allots the residence to the workman. Learned counsel for workman has submitted that 
since the workman was entitled to one accommodation which was not being provided by the management inspite of 
the fact that there were vacant accommodations available and there were incidences of such nature earlier also, in 
which the workers broke open the vacant accommodation and took possession of the accommodations without 
allotment, the workman could not be held guilty of the misconduct. 


I am not inclined to accept this argument on the ground that if the workman was not allotted any 
accommodation, he would be getting house rent allowances and only entitlement does not gave anyone license to 
commit illegality. Thus, when there is clear evidence that the workman illegally occupied the accommodation without 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 10, 2026/पौष 20, 1947 7837 


allotment, he cannot be exonerated from the charge only on the ground that he was entitled to get one accommodation 
and accommodations were vacant. Hence, in light of above discussion, the charge of misconduct is held proved 
against the workman. 


Issue No. 1 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2, 


Workman has been awarded punishment of permanent stoppage of one increment and recovery of penal rent 
from him as well pay of suspension period has also not been given to him by way of punishment. Learned counsel for 
workman has submitted that this is an excessive punishment compared to the charges. His main grievance is with 
respect to permanent stoppage of one increment in the punishment order which is its replicating effect. 


On the other hand, it has been submitted by learned counsel for management that the workman is a habitual 
offender, he has committed misconduct earlier also for which he has been punished. Hence, keeping in view these 
facts the punishment order cannot be said to be an excessive one. He further submits that the punishment order does 
not warrant any interference. 


Settled proposition of law is that the punishment is domain of Executive and Courts and Tribunals, who be 
hesitant in interfering with the punishment orders until and unless they are satisfied, it is so disproportionate that it 
shocks the conscious of the Court or Tribunal. 


To consider whether the punishment order is shockingly disproportionate to the charge, the nature and effect 
of the misconduct proved, previous conduct will entirely be the factors to be considered. 


In the case in hand, undisputedly, the workman has a history of misconduct. Permanent stoppage of 
increment has its replicating effect and it harms the workman till his superannuation and also thereafter. The workman 
was entitled to accommodation from the management which were vacated at the time of misconduct but the process 
adopted by workman was not a correct way of enforcing his rights. This fact that after another accommodation was 
allotted to him, the workman vacated the said accommodation which he had occupied forcibly, the punishment of 
cumulative stoppage appears too harsh. Hence, keeping in this fact, the sentence of cumulative stoppage of one 
increment is converted into stoppage of one increment for five years and the punishment stands modified accordingly. 


Issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly. 
In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.- 
AWARD 


“Holding the action of the General Manager, Central Workshop, Jayant Project of NCL, in imposing 
punishment of Suspension, Stoppage of increment & Penal rent, on an alleged misconduct of illegal occupying of 
the quarter by Shri J.P. Singh, Fitter (vacated during the course of enquiry proceedings), excessive, the stoppage of 
one increment with cumulative effect is converted into stoppage of one increment for five years.” 


No order as to cost.

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment vide its Order No. L-14011/15/2018-IR(DU) 
dated 27.11.2018 referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Con..2 
The schedule mentioned in that order is: 


“Whether the action of the management of Indian Coast Guard, Base Maintenance Unit, Chennai, in 
transferring Sh. P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter to [CGS Mandapam in an non-existing post at ICGS 
Mandapam is legal and justified? If not, to what relief Sh. P.Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter is entitled 
to?” 


As per the claim statement the petitioner is an Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union, registered under the 
Trade Union Act, 1926 was formed primarily to protect the interest of the workmen and for the welfare of the 
employees apart from maintaining harmonious relationship with the Management. It is submitted that there are 60 
civilian workmen in the establishment and most of them are members of the Union, this being the only union

functioning in the establishment to espouse the cause of the workmen. It is submitted that the Union raised an 
Industrial Dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C) by letter dated 21.11.2017 under Section 2(K) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act,1947 over the issue relating to the unfair labour practices adopted by the respondent 
Management. It is submitted that the union was registered on 07.07.2017 vide Regn. No.508/TVR under the Trade 
Unions Act, 1947 and thereafter in the General Body Meeting the office bearers were elected. It is submitted that the 
fact relating to the registration of the union and the list of elected office bearers was communicated to the respondent 
Management by letter No.ICGEU/BMU/01/2017, dated 15.07.2017. 


2. It is submitted that the 1 respondent has framed the “Transfer Policy-Civilian” by letter no.CP/0518 dated 
22.11.2006 and circulated to the Regional Commanders for compliance. Para 4(c) deals with Group ‘B’ ‘C’ ‘D’ 
Non-Gazetted personal, wherein it is clearly stated that postings and transfer of these employees are to be kept at 
absolute minimum level keeping in view the administrative requirement and need for manning the posts at various 
stations. It has also been clearly mentioned that in case of transfers being inescapable, volunteers for the postings or 
transfer will be called. As far as possible only volunteers will be transferred to these vacancies. It has also been 
clearly stated that as far as possible the group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employee should not be transferred over long distance 
and efforts should be made to accommodate them near their choice station to the extent possible. 


3. As per the above, Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was elected as Treasurer of the union. Since the Respondent / 
Management was against the formation of the union, the employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was relieved and directed 
to report for duty at ICGS, Mandapam by letter No.CP/277/17, dated 31.10.2017 


4. The transfer order dated 20.10.2017 was not served on the workman till date. While the petitioner union requested 
that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj be declared a protected workman, but the Management swiftly reacted by transferring 
Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj and victimized him by adopting unfair labour practice. Hence requested the following relief. 


i) To declare that the transfer order bearing no.1340 dated 20.10.2017 issued by the 37 Respondent 
transferring Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to Indian Coast 
Guard Station, Mandapam is not justified as per the guidelines laid down by the 1“ respondent in the Transfer 
Policy CP/0518 dated 22.11.2006 


ii) And to pass such other award/order as this Hon’ble Central Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour 
Court may deem fit and necessary in the circumstances of the case and thus render justice.

5. The respondent in its reply stated that the Indian Coast Guard Civilian Employees Union has not been recognized 
by the Ministry of Defence, as per CGHA letter WE/0302/Welfare dated 09.10.2019.The transfer order of the three 
(3) civilian personal was promulgated vide CGRHQ(E) letter 1340 dated 20.10.17. Accordingly, the individual was 
relieved from Basic Maintenance Unit, Chennai to report at Indian Coast Guard Station, Madapam as per the 
transfer policy and pleaded that the petition be dismissed as devoid of merit. 


6. The Respondent filed the following documents in support of their contention 


Exhibit No. Date Description 

Ex.M1 18.04.2018 Nature of duties carried out by Indian Coast Guard Base 
Maintenance Unit (Chennai) 

Ex.M2 09.10.2019 Service Association and Welfare in Indian Coast Guard 

Ex.M3 22.11.2006 Transfer Policy - Civilians 


7. Heard both learned counsel and perused the records. The point arised for determination is whether the transfer of 
Shri P. Ayan Aurl Raj, Radio/Radar Fitter as ICGS, Mandapam is an not existing post at ICGS, Mandapam is legal 
and justify? If not, what relief is Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj, Radio/Radar fitter is entitled to? 


8. The claimant in its claim statement stated that the following points regarding the transfer policy. 


(a) Posting and transfer are to be kept at the absolute minimum level 
(b) Volunteers for the postings of the transfer called and will be transferred 
(c) Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ employees should not be transferred over long distance 


9. In petition claim the hardships caused to transferring described as under 


(a) Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred during October,2017 quite impossible for getting admission for his 
school going children at the new station 

(b) The workman unable to shift his family in the midst of the academic year 

(c) The employee kept the family in Chennai for his child to complete the studies in the academic year but the 
Estate Office, CPWD directed him to vacate the quarters and threatened to impose a penalty 

(d) The employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fell sick because of the mental agony and remains on leave on medical 
ground from 1.11.2017 to 28.6.2018 

(e) When the workman reported for duty on 29.06.2018 at the Mandapam station, the 31 Respondent directed 


him to report for duty in Chennai for four days in a week. 


10. On perusal of whole the claim statement, the claimant nowhere stated that Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj was transferred 
to a non-existing post at ICGS Mandapam. On perusal of the claim statement, it appears that the Respondent did not 
violate the transfer policy, as the Mandapam station is not far away from Chennai station. 


11. It is the fundamental duty of transferring employee to seek the permission to overstay at Govt. accommodation by 
mentioning the sufficient reasons for occupation of the allotted house. In claim petition this facts nowhere mention 
that any application mentioning sufficient reasons for over staying at the allotted house was made or not. In this 
situation it can be presumed that no application was made by the transferring employee to the authority. 
Transferring employee Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj fails to submit the medical certificates which might have established 
the genuine grounds of his absence due to medical reasons. 


12. It is stated in the claim petition that the employee was transferred due to his involvement in the union, but the 
claimant fails to submit any evidence that may establish this fact that respondent had showed its jealous against the 
employee. The only vague reason given is that he was an elected as an office bearer in the union, the transfer of an 
employee do not appear as a result of his election to the union. 


13. The claimant has stated that no transfer order was provided to the transferred employee and that only a relieving 
order was provided to the transferee employee. The relieving order issued to Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj dated 
31.10.2017 is available at page no.2 of the paper book in this document, it is mentioned clearly that the Competent 
Authority has approved the transfer of Shri P. Ayan Arul Raj with a direction to report at ICGS Mandapam by 
10.11.2017. The relieving order was issued by the Section Officer in compliance with the order passed by the 
Competent Authority hence, no right of the transfree employee was violated by not providing a separate transfer 
order. 


14. As per the discussion above, the transfer order was not made by the Respondent in violation of transfer policy or

by or on behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In 
such a situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead 
evidence to establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, 
who would fail if no evidence is led.”’

Further it has been pleaded by the respondent in their written statement as under:-

b). The Learned Regional Labour Commissioner, Lucknow, without proper application of mind, contrary to the 
settled principles of law acting like a postman send the report to the Central Government for referring the matter for

c). As per the provisions of section 2 A sub section (3), of the Industrial Disputes’ Act, 1947, any application for 
adjudicating any dispute or difference between a workman and his employer connected with, or arising out of

discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination shall be made to the Labour Court or Tribunal before the expiry of 
three years from the date of such discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination. 


d). A limitation of three years for raising an industrial dispute has been provided in the Industrial Disputes' Act, 1947,

On behalf of respondent evidence on affidavit of Shri Ashotosh Anand, Chief Manager, HRM of the bank filed, he 
was cross examined on 04.05.2015. 


On behalf of workman on 27.06.2016 rejoinder affidavit has been filed denying the averments as taken by respondent. 


On 05.11.2020, workman/claimant has filed evidence on affidavit (Examination in Chief) and he was cross examined 
on 07.01.2021, by respondent. 


During the pendency of case as per notification dated 26.11.2019, moved by the Ministry Of Finance (Department of 
Financial Services), relevant portion quoted herein below:- 


Baroda Uttar Pradesh Gramin Bank, Kashi Gomti Samyut Gramin Bank and Purvanchal Bank (hereinafter 
referred to as "the transferor Regional Rural Banks") sponsored by the Bank of Baroda, Union Bank of India 
and State Bank of India in the State of Uttar Pradesh are hereby amalgamated into a single Regional Rural 
Bank which shall be called as Baroda U.P. Bank (hereinafter referred to as "the transferee Regional Rural 
Bank") with its head office at Gorakhpur under the sponsorship of Bank of Baroda. 


Accordingly as per the said notification respondent 10.1 0 & 1B were imp leaded as party, In view of the law laid 
down by Hon’ble Madras High Court in case of Palanisamy R vs. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, 2001 
LawSuit(Mad) 152, and also in the case of Shri Kanchi Kamakoti Peetam Charitable Trust Hospital vs. Industrial 
Tribunal & Others, 2004 (100) FLR 1166. 


I have heard Shri Parvez Alam legal representative of claimant, and Shri Adarsh Jagdhari learned counsel for 
respondent. 


After hearing the parties/their legal representative and Advocate, the first point to be considered the point to be 
consider in the present case:- 


A). whether the reference dated 17.02.2015, is vague and on the basis of the same no cause of action arises on the 
part of workman/claimant to file present claim petition. 


In order to decide the said dispute it would be appropriate to go through Section 10 of the Industrial Dispute Act. 
10. Section 10 of Industrial Disputes Act reads thus: 


"10. Reference of disputes to Boards, Courts or Tribunals. (1) [Where the appropriate Government is of 
opinion that any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, it may at any time), by order in writing,- 


(a) refer the dispute to a Board for promoting a settlement thereof; or 
(b) refer any matter appearing to be connected with or relevant to the dispute to a Court for inquiry; or 


[(c) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, if it relates to 
any matter specified in the Second Schedule, to a Labour Court for adjudication; or 


(d) refer the dispute or any matter appearing to be connected with, or relevant to, the dispute, whether it 
relates to any matter specified in the Second Schedule or the Third Schedule, to a Tribunal for adjudication: 


Provided that where the dispute relates to any matter specified in the Third Schedule and is not likely to 
affect more than one hundred workmen, the appropriate Government may, if it so thinks fit, make the 
reference to a Labour Court under clause (c):]" 


11. Plain reading of aforesaid provision would show that when industrial dispute exists or is apprehended, appropriate 
Government can refer dispute to Court for enquiry or if relates to any matter specified in Second Schedule to Labour 
Court for adjudication or make Reference to Tribunal, if dispute relates to matters specified in Second Schedule or 
Third Schedule. It is, therefore, obvious that Reference can be made only when industrial disputes exists or is 
apprehended by Competent Authority. 


13. The aforesaid legal position would make explicit that existence of industrial dispute is a paramount and important 
consideration while dealing with Reference. 


Only existent or apprehended industrial disputes can be referred for consideration of Court or Tribunal. However, at 
the time of taking decision whether Reference to be made or not, appropriate Government need not venture into 


4068 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 9, 2026/VAISAKHA 19, 1948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


merits of dispute, as making Reference is only administrative function. Only because Reference is made under 
Section 10(1), Court or Tribunal is not precluded from entering into aspects of delay and laches or to record findings 
as to existence or non-existence of dispute. 


In case of Prabhakar v. Joint Director, Sericulture Department and "another, 2015 (147) FLR 341 (SC), the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court considered and held the impact of delay and laches in Reference made under Section 10(1) of 
Industrial Disputes Act and observed in paragraph No. 14 as under: 


"40. An industrial dispute has to be referred by the appropriate Government for adjudication and the 
workman cannot approach the Labour Court or Industrial Tribunal directly, except in those cases which are 
covered by Section 2-A of the Act. Reference is made under Section 10 of the Act in those cases where the 
appropriate Government forms an opinion that ‘any industrial dispute exists or is apprehended’. The words 
‘industrial dispute exists' are of paramount importance unless there is an existence of an industrial dispute 
(or the dispute is apprehended or it is apprehended such a dispute may arise in near future), no reference is 
to be made. Thus, existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute is a sine qua non for making the 
reference. No doubt, at the time of taking a decision whether a reference is to be made or not, the 
appropriate Government is not to go into the merits of the dispute. Making of reference is only an 
administrative function. At the same time, on the basis of material on record, satisfaction of the existence of 
the industrial dispute or the apprehension of an industrial dispute is necessary. Such existence/apprehension 
of industrial dispute, thus, becomes a condition precedent, though it will be only subjective satisfaction 
based on material on record. Since, we are not concerned with the satisfaction dealing with cases where 
there is apprehended industrial dispute, discussion that follows would confine to existence of an industrial 
dispute. Dispute or difference arises when one party make a demand and other party rejects the same. It is 
held by this Court in number of cases that before raising the industrial dispute making of demand is a 
necessary pre-condition. In such a scenario, if the services of a workman are terminated and he does not 
make the demand and/or raise the issue alleging wrongful termination immediately thereafter or within 
reasonable time and raises the same after considerable lapse of period, whether it can be said that industrial 
dispute still exist. Since there is no period of limitation, it gives right to the workman to raise the dispute 
even belatedly. However, if the dispute is raised after a long period, it has to be seen as to whether such a 
dispute still exists? Thus, notwithstanding the fact that law of limitation does not apply, it is to be shown by 
the workman that there is a dispute in praesenti. For this purpose, he has to demonstrate that even if 
considerable period has lapsed and there are laches and delays, such delay has not resulted into making the 
industrial dispute seized to exist. Therefore, if the workman is able to give satisfactory explanation for these 
laches and delays and demonstrate that the circumstances discloses that issue is still alive, delay would not 
come in his way because of the reason that law of limitation has no application. On the other hand, if 
because of such delay dispute no longer remains alive and is to be treated as "dead", then it would be non- 
existent dispute which cannot be referred." 


Thus it can be held on the point in issue that for raising industrial dispute demand is precondition. In case, employee 
fails to make demand, dispute cannot be referred. 


From the perusal of claim statement filed by claimant on 06.05.2005, undisputed facts which emerged out that he was 
initially appointed as casual labour on the post of jamadaar cum chaprasi in the purvanchal gramin bank, Gorakhpur, 
now known as Baroda UP bank, in the branch saleempur dewaria, in the said capacity he worked and discharged his 
duties up till 29.04.2006, his services were retrenched/terminated, so workman raise a Industrial Dispute and by 
reference dated 17.02.2015, the same was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication quoted here an above.

By order No. K-10/2/2022-IR dated 21.10.2022 the present industrial dispute has been referred for 
adjudication to this Tribunal in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) 
of Section 10 the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) by the Central Government, with following schedule: 


"Whether the action of the management of North Eastern Railway, Gorakhpur and Lucknow in terminating 
the services of Shri Krishna Chandra Dwivedi, Casual Labour w.e.f. 31.12.1976 is justified and legal? If not 
to what relief the workman is entitled to” 


Accordingly, an industrial dispute No. 12/2024 has been registered on 24.04.2024. 


From the perusal of record, the position which emerge out is that the till date the claimant/workman has not filed any 
statement of claim in spite of repeated opportunity given to him, in order to establish his claim, as per the reference 
dated 21.10.2022. 


So in view of the said facts, as well as the law laid by the Hon’ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. 
Labour Court (I) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


“Tt is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality 
of the order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a 
workman raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file 
written statement before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must 
also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce 
evidence, the dispute referred by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he 
would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. 
Raj Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) FLR 38 
and Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on 
behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a 
situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to 
establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail 
if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A 
perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the 
respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


As the workman has not filed any statement of claim/oral/documentary evidence, so the present case is liable to be 
dismissed. 


For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and; and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Award as above.

1.Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along 
with continuity of service and full back wages. 


2.It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai karamchari 
on 04.09.2016 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But the said 
minimum wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% ESI 
and Rs.300/- as TDS from hissalary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under the ambit of taxfree 
limit. He was working under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to avoid its liability always 
shows his employment in record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


3.It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent 10.1. However, their demand was not 
accepted. Other workers working under respondent 10.1 formed union and subsequently his services were 
dispensed with w.e.f. 27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also 
made fresh appointments after termination of his services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of 
the Act. Thus, there is violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4.Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5.Respondent 10.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate 
as prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non- 
Cantonment Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering 
respondent entered into contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). 
In July 2018, the answering respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and 
M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e-tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide 
conservancy services in Chandi Mandir Military Station for the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no. 2 
submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed their duties and answering respondent is 
only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command Chandigarh to release payment directly to 
the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is 
carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent has no responsibility of 
disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed 
union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the premises of 
Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent asked 
respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the 
answering respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the 
answering respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative 
office of the Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union 
unauthorizedly and indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor

and therefore, termination is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6.Respondent 10.2 also filed reply maintaining therein that workman worked with it w.e.f. 05.07.2018 to

WWI/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on 
30.07.2024.

Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex.MW1/A along with

Submissions of workman:- 


10. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by 
respondent 10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by 
respondent 10.1 on 04.09.2016 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any 
reason in violation of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and 
junior to him were retained in service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So 
far as the agreements between the respondent 10.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair 
labour practice. The work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having 
any license. The contractor has left after three months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the 
service of the workman, which is mandatory under the Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


11. On the other hand, AR for respondent no.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 
no.2 (contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent 10.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between respondent 10.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the 
respondent 10.2 to the workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the 
services of the workman. Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of 
the Act, then it is done by respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to 
EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not 
permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent 10.1 being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of 
his appointment by respondent 10.2 and has filed a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the 
workman is not maintainable. 


12. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


Findings:- 


13. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing 
his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to 
perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 


Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has observed as follows:- 
“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 


employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are 
not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the

meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract 
basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be 
inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman.” 


14. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any 
distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in 
plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In 
view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein 
admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


15. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 


Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


16. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in 
the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, 
salary, letter of appointment by respondent no.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature 
for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally 
lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P 
Singh in his cross examination has stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the 
conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to 
the conservancy staff. Contractor is responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has no roll in terminating the services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who 
was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 


17. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. 
Ex.R-2 is the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges 
that workman was paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. 
Thus, there does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 
10.1. However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


18. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was 
supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, respondent 10.2 would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


19. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 
1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) 


of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. 
The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 
(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to 
calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was 
doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was 
cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for 
rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent no.2 would be termed as industry. 


20. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G 
and 25H of the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 04.09.2016 and he was paid minimum wages 
prescribed by Central Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any 
compensation before terminating his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated 
that his salary used to be credited in his bank account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in 
which his salary was credited in order to enable this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. 
However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from

the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis 
were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with respondent no.1. Thus, workman was employee of 
respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed above. There does not exist any relationship 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists relation of 
employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 


21. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as 
regards violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the 
workman. Hence, workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 


22. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by 
respondent 10.1 by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement 
executed between respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions 
of AR for workman that the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry 
was held before terminating the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that 
workman was entitled only for compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and 
no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not 
mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a 
department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that regular recruitment procedure is 
provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is not employee of 
respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


23. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not 
working with respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary 
given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, 
this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 
24. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of 
compensation is deemed fit by this Tribunal: 

Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 

Rs.30,000/-. 


Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


25. Present workman employed on 04.09.2016 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 2 years 
but less than 5 years), so he is entitled for Rs.30,000/-. 
26. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.30,000/- within one month from the date of the 


notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the 
date of award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent no.1 requires safai 
karamcharis, then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.
